title: An exception table read with an inclusive end_pc hands an exception to the wrong handler
summary: The interpreter finds the handler for a thrown exception in the `Code` attribute's exception table: the first entry, in table order, whose range covers the pc of the throwing instruction. The range is `[start_pc, end_pc)`, and the specification itself calls the exclusive end a historical mistake. A developer building a JVM decides not to repeat the mistake and makes the end inclusive, so that a handler can cover the last instruction of a method. The property the build proves of the lookup, stated over the table's columns as arrays, is refuted on a table with an entry whose `end_pc` is the pc of the throwing instruction, which the patched lookup hands to a handler that does not cover it.

change.description: Treat `end_pc` as inclusive: an entry covers `start_pc <= pc <= end_pc`. The class comment now says that this implementation does not repeat the historical mistake JVMS §4.7.3 describes, so that a handler can cover the last instruction of a method's code. The tests for the lookup pass.

risk: Every class file ever compiled was written for the exclusive `end_pc`: javac emits `end_pc` as the pc of the first instruction after the protected block, which is where the handler's own code, or the code after the `try`, begins. Read inclusively, an exception thrown by that first instruction is handled by a block it was never inside: a `catch` clause that rethrows now catches the exception thrown while it was itself running, a `finally` block's first instruction loops into its own handler, and an exception thrown right after a `try` is swallowed by it. The tests cover pcs inside, before and after the ranges, and the one pc that changed is the end itself, which nobody thought to test because nothing is supposed to be there.
explanation: The property committed for `handlerIndex` is stated over the columns of the table, two arrays the prover fills with every content up to eight entries: when the result is an index, the entry at it covers the pc, `startPc[result] <= pc && pc < endPc[result]`. JBMC finds a refutation at once: a table with an entry whose `end_pc` equals the pc, which the patched lookup returns although the entry does not cover it; the tool replays the input in its interpreter and shows the index returned. The witness is the boundary the specification defines, and the property as committed is the sentence of §4.7.3 the change set out to correct. Two halves of the full specification are not in the property, and the file says why: that the entry is the first in table order, and that -1 comes only when no entry covers the pc, are quantifiers that repeat the scan's own comparisons, and JBMC's SAT backend did not finish them in minutes on tables of four entries, while the half above is proved of the unpatched lookup in under a second. The property states what the solver can check, and the comment records what it could not, which is itself the kind of statement a reviewer wants to see.
resolution: Revert. A virtual machine implements the class-file format as it is, mistakes included, because the format is a contract with every compiler that ever targeted it; a handler that covers the last instruction of a method is the compiler's problem to avoid, and javac avoids it. The property stays as the regression test for the next person who reads §4.7.3's admission as an invitation.
provenance: Constructed from the note in JVMS §4.7.3 that the exclusivity of end_pc is a historical mistake in the design of the Java Virtual Machine, by acting on it.

references.title: JVMS §4.7.3, the Code attribute: the exception table, and the fact that end_pc is exclusive is a historical mistake
JVMS §2.10, exceptions: the handlers are searched in the order they appear in the table
